title: Towards a Formal Definition of Agent Memory: Basis, Span, Optimality, and the Sequential Memory Problem

analysis.tldr: The paper proposes a representation-agnostic formalism in which stored events form a memory basis, a generation operator defines its knowledge span, memory quality becomes query coverage under a capacity budget, and sequential writing becomes an MDP with delayed query-time reward.
analysis.problem: Agent-memory systems use incompatible representations and metrics, so memory quality is hard to compare and the optimal write problem is rarely stated explicitly.
analysis.core_idea: Separate stored events from the knowledge they generate via an operator Phi. Under a single-item-support assumption, answerability becomes coverage over the memory's span; capacity-constrained optimal memory traces a utility-capacity frontier. Noisy extraction separates coverage from precision, and unknown future query distributions motivate a sequential memorization MDP.

memory_design.write: A write policy selects a bounded subset of events from material; in the sequential formulation, writing is an action whose value is revealed later by query-time utility.
memory_design.organize: Memory is the event basis; its semantic span is Phi(memory). Under noise, stored claims are separated into asserted span versus good/true span. The formalism deliberately abstracts away graph/page/vector layout.
memory_design.read: A read policy retrieves a subset of the span for a query. The main theory uses single-item support, pushing composition into Phi rather than answer-time multi-item reasoning.
memory_design.update_forget: The sequential MDP allows memory state to change as queries arrive under a capacity constraint, but the paper does not propose a concrete replacement/forgetting algorithm.

compared_to: Representative agent-memory systems are positioned in a common formal write/read/reasoning framework rather than empirically outperformed
analysis.evidence: The main evidence is theoretical: the utility-capacity frontier is non-decreasing and saturates at the full-context baseline under monotonicity; with decomposable Phi, optimal writing reduces to weighted maximum coverage with the classical greedy (1-1/e) approximation, while cross-event synergy breaks that guarantee. An Odyssey case study is illustrative rather than a broad empirical validation.
analysis.why_it_matters: If the assumptions are useful, the utility-capacity frontier provides a cleaner way to compare memory systems at matched capacity and separates what is stored, what knowledge it spans, and how well a reasoner uses it.
limitations: Single-item support rules out answer-time composition; all multi-event reasoning must already be materialized inside the generation operator.
Coverage is explicitly not correctness, and the theory treats reasoner failures as a separate layer.
Monotonicity and self-containment are only approximate for real LLM extraction; conflicting memories can violate them.

The formalism is representation-agnostic and empirically illustrated on a hand-checked Odyssey instance, so it does not establish that the proposed yardstick predicts real agent performance across modern memory architectures.
